Spinal disk herniation

Three trials of high-intensity laser reported short-term functional or symptom improvements, including sham-controlled lumbar results and benefits after collagenase at one month but not three or six months. In a low-level-laser trial, laser was similar to placebo on several outcomes while LED improved some measures.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Three trials of high-intensity laser reported short-term functional or symptom improvements, including sham-controlled lumbar results and benefits after collagenase at one month but not three or six months. In a low-level-laser trial, laser was similar to placebo on several outcomes while LED improved some measures.

Summary of the Evidence

Four unique human clinical publications examine spinal disc herniation: two randomized HILT trials, one non-randomized HILT active-comparator study, and one randomized low-level laser, LED, and placebo study. The studies include lumbar and cervical diagnoses, use different co-interventions, and do not represent four independent tests of one uniform PBM protocol. No animal or laboratory publication was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

A sham-controlled trial of lumbar HILT plus exercise reported reduced MRI disc dimensions, pain, and disability over six weeks compared with sham plus the same exercise. A second lumbar trial found that HILT added to collagenase improved pain, disability, and health-related quality of life at one week and one month, but the between-group advantage was not present at three or six months. In a cervical disc herniation comparison study, HILT and active TENS/ultrasound both improved symptoms. The low-level laser/LED trial found laser outcomes similar to placebo for several measures, whereas LED was better on some pain and function outcomes (Mohammed et al. 2026 Song et al. 2025 Yilmaz et al. 2020 de Carvalho et al. 2016).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified for this indication.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or tissue study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The HILT protocols used high-power near-infrared devices; the 2025 lumbar study reports 890 and 910 nm, 15 W, and 10 J/cm² over five daily sessions. The 2026 sham-controlled study also tested HILT with exercise. The low-level-laser study used 904 nm laser and 945 nm LED with positioning and flexion exercises. Intensity, diagnosis, comparator, and treatment schedules differ, so their effects should not be combined as one dose estimate.

Interpretation

The strongest findings concern short-term adjunctive HILT, with one study showing no sustained between-group advantage after one month. Low-level laser has not clearly outperformed placebo in the mapped trial.

Evidence strength in source summaryShort-term pain and function with mixed laser regimens: Low Low-level laser versus placebo: Very low
Publications and records4 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Four human trials provide more evidence than neighboring spinal categories, but three use high-intensity laser and the fourth combines low-level laser or LED with exercise. Short follow-up, co-interventions, and different spinal levels limit pooling. The sham-controlled low-level-laser result was not clearly better than placebo. Replicated trials with common outcomes and longer follow-up are needed.
